title: Percentages and Ratios
objectives: Understand ratios as comparisons between quantities and their real-world applications
Create and identify equivalent ratios through scaling and simplification
Convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages fluently
Calculate percentage increases and decreases in practical contexts
Connect ratios and percentages to solve proportional reasoning problems

introduction.context: Percentages and ratios help us make sense of how things relate to each other, turning tricky comparisons into everyday tools for figuring things out, making choices, and tackling real-life puzzles. This section pulls together what you've learned so far: place value and decimals from the Decimals Basics section give you the groundwork for working out percentages (like 25% = 0.25), fractions from the Fractions Basics section match up nicely (50% = 1/2), and the operations from the Addition and Subtraction, Multiplication Basics, and Division Basics sections let you calculate ratios or spot percentage shifts.
introduction.connection: Picture a shop owner eyeing sales: ratios show how well things balance, percentages highlight changes - both grew from old-time ways of weighing up value. Over the years, these ideas came from needs in buying, taxing, and studying the world.
introduction.historicalContext: The Babylonians around 1800 BCE scratched ratios on clay for splitting family goods (say, 2:3 shares), and their number setup made easy splits for star tracking. The ancient Egyptians in 2000 BCE used ratios for building pyramids, with simple setups like 3:4:5 for straight corners, and early percentages from fractions for taxes (a tenth skimmed off). The Greeks took it further: Pythagoras in 500 BCE checked ratios in music strings (2:1 for an octave jump), and Euclid in 300 BCE explained ratios as size match-ups in his big book, proving shapes line up. Romans borrowed for building: Vitruvius around 1st century BCE set rules like column height to width. The word 'percent' comes from Latin 'per centum' (per hundred), popping up in 1400s Italy for loan fees (5 per cento = 5%). Fibonacci's 1202 math book tossed in ratio challenges for traders, like blending metals. By the 1500s, percentages locked in for banks, and Simon Stevin in 1585 tied them to decimals for smoother work. The % mark grew from shorthand in 1600s notes. In the 1700s, Euler wove ratios into growth math, and 1800s stats (like body size indexes as ratios) plus money talk made percentages key for numbers like price hikes. Today, ratios shape screens (width:height) and polls use percentages.
introduction.realWorldApplications: In daily life, they size up connections. Percentages: deals (20% off $50 saves $10), scores (85% right), boosts (5% extra cash). Ratios: baking (2:1 flour to water), maps (1:100 for distances), bets (3:1 odds). Health: weight to height squared for body mass. Business: profit slice as percentage. These link back - ratios use fraction steps from the Fractions Basics section, percentages divide by 100 like decimals.

concepts.title: 7.1 Understanding Ratios
concepts.content: Ratios size up amounts side by side, like blending juice: 2 cups water to 3 cups concentrate - the mix, not the full jug. This side-by-side or part-of-whole view makes ratios different from plain counts. In straightforward terms, a ratio a:b means a to b, or a/b - the link between a and b (keep the order unless they're the same). Step by step: Hands-on - grab counters: 4 apples to 6 oranges = 4:6. Next, jot as fraction 4/6, but remember ratios compare, fractions stand for bits. Deeper - speeds: 60 miles in 2 hours = 30:1 miles per hour. From history, Babylonians mixed recipes with ratios (1:2 for metal blends). Greeks like Aristotle in 300 BCE saw ratios as balanced pairs. Uses: Games - hit rate 3:10. Money - debt to pay 1:3. Mix-ups: Ratios as sums - clear it's about match (2:3 ≠5); flip order - 3:2 ≠2:3, try examples. Build: Hands-on items. Speeds next. Unit links (cost per one). Example: Squad wins 5, drops 3 - 5:3.

commonMisconceptions: Thinking ratios represent totals (2:3 doesn't mean 5 items)

concepts.title: 7.2 Equivalent Ratios and Simplifying
concepts.content: Equivalent ratios keep the same balance but scaled, like 2:4 = 1:2 - same feel, just bigger. Picture doubling a 1:2 mix to 2:4 - tastes the same. In clear terms, a:b = c:d if a/d = b/c (cross-check ad=bc); trim by shared factors. Step by step: Hands-on - make charts: 1:3, times 2=2:6, times 3=3:9. Next, trim: 4:12 split by 4=1:3. Deeper - find gap: 2:5 = x:15, x=6 (cross). History: Euclid showed matches for shapes. Old traders for coins. Uses: Maps - 1:100000 same as stretched miles. Meals - food ratios grown. Mix-ups: Sum to trim - off (4:6 ≠5:7); check with times. Build: Hands-on grows. Trim next. Solve gaps. Example: 10:15 = 2:3 trimmed.

developmentStages.semiAbstract: Apply cross multiplication to check equivalence
developmentStages.abstract: Use GCD to simplify complex ratios systematically

commonMisconceptions: Adding same number to both parts (1:2 ≠ 2:3)
Not simplifying ratios to lowest terms

concepts.title: 7.3 Understanding Percentages
concepts.content: Percentages are ratios out of 100, easy like 50% = 50/100=1/2 - half full. Shade half a 100-grid square. In plain speak, p% = p/100; turn fraction f to % by f×100. Step by step: Hands-on - percent bar: Shade 25% =1/4. Next, switch: 3/5=0.6=60%. Deeper - spot: 20% of 150=30 (0.2×150). History: Romans took 'per hundred' for dues (8 per hundred). 1400s Italy shorted it; % from 1650. Uses: Tips - 15% on $40=$6. Votes - 60% yes. Mix-ups: % as sum - 20% + 30% ≠50% on different starts; sort it. Build: Hands-on bars. Switches next. Parts deeper. Example: 40% of 50=20.

concepts.title: 7.4 Percentage Increase and Decrease
concepts.content: Percentage shift tracks relative move: up from 100 to 120=20% gain. Picture a sale: 20% cut - times by 0.8. In terms, shift = (new - old)/old ×100%; down is minus. Step by step: Hands-on - bar grow: 50 up 20%=10 more, 60 total. Next, formula: 80 down 25%=(80×0.25)=20 less, 60. Deeper - stack: 100 +10% =110, then -5%=110×0.95=104.5. History: 1700s money folks for ups. Stats set it. Uses: Price rise - 3% more. Shares - 5% dip. Mix-ups: Shifts add - 50% up then down ≠ start (100+50=150-75=75); math it out. Build: Hands-on easy. Stack next. Back-shift (80 to 100=25% up?). Example: 200 down 15%=30 less=170.

developmentStages.concrete: Use visual bars to show before and after values
developmentStages.semiAbstract: Apply percentage change formulas to real scenarios
developmentStages.abstract: Understand compound percentage changes don't commute

commonMisconceptions: Using wrong base for percentage calculation
Thinking percentage changes are commutative (50% up then 50% down ≠ original)

concepts.title: 7.5 Relating Percentages and Ratios
concepts.content: Percentages are ratios to 100, say 2:5=40:100=40%. Picture ratio 3:7 as (3/10)×100=30%, rest 70%. In terms, ratio a:b to % - (a/(a+b))×100 for a, same for b. Step by step: Hands-on - sketch: 2:3=40%,60%. Next, switch: 1:4=20%? Wait, 1:4=25:100=25%. Deeper - fix: Ratio 3:2, first %=(3/5)×100=60%. History: 1500s tied for balances. New stats use. Uses: Charts - ratios as %. Blends - 2:3 mix=40% one. Mix-ups: Ratio straight to % - 1:2≠1%, but 33.3:66.7%. Build: Hands-on switches. Parts next. Puzzles deeper. Example: Ratio 5:3, first %=5/8×100=62.5%. In short: Ratios match, percentages level - pair up strong.

developmentStages.abstract: Apply ratio-percentage relationships to solve complex problems

commonMisconceptions: Converting ratio parts directly to percentages (1:2 ≠ 1% and 2%)
Forgetting percentages from ratios must sum to 100%

examples.problem: In a fruit bowl, there are 4 apples and 6 oranges. What is the ratio of apples to oranges?
examples.solution: The ratio of apples to oranges is 4:6, which can be simplified to 2:3

examples.problem: A price increases from $50 to $60. What is the percentage increase?

practice.problem: What is the ratio of 12 to 18 in simplest form?
practice.explanation: Divide both 12 and 18 by their GCD of 6 to get 2:3
hints: Find the greatest common divisor of 12 and 18
Divide both numbers by the GCD

practice.problem: If the ratio of cats to dogs is 4:7, and there are 28 dogs, how many cats are there?
practice.explanation: Set up proportion: 4:7 = x:28. Cross multiply: 7x = 4×28 = 112, so x = 16

practice.problem: A population increases from 200 to 250. What is the percentage increase?
If the ratio is 2:3, what percentage does the first part represent?
hints: Find the total number of parts
Calculate what fraction the first part represents
